title: Researchers Say They’ve Found the Truth About Thomas Jefferson
excerpt: T hree hours after Thomas Jefferson died at his Monticello home on July 4, 1826, his personal secretary, Nicholas Trist, snipped a lock of the Founder’s gray ha
body: T hree hours after Thomas Jefferson died at his Monticello home on July 4, 1826, his personal secretary, Nicholas Trist, snipped a lock of the Founder’s gray hair, still faintly reddish blond
Trist then tied the hair with orange thread and placed it in a paper packet, along with a short note describing what he’d done
In an era before photography or modern embalming, hair was an easily preserved reminder of a beloved friend or relative who’d died

Trist did not know that he was also securing physical evidence that, two centuries later, would help resolve one of the nation’s oldest and most contentious historical debates: whether the author of the Declaration of Independence, the nation’s third president, had children with Sally Hemings, a woman he enslaved for half a century and never freed

After a covert and exhaustive 15-year effort led by the Smithsonian Institution, a team of geneticists, genealogists, historians, and anthropologists believe it has found proof that Jefferson fathered at least two of Hemings’s six children
On Tuesday, Richard Kurin, a Smithsonian cultural anthropologist, who led the multidisciplinary research effort, will publish a book detailing the team’s findings
A scientific paper is currently under review for publication in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences ( PNAS )
The researchers, who agreed to speak with me about their results before publication, relied on the latest genetic techniques to reassemble Jefferson’s genome from the Founder’s hair

They then matched that sequence with DNA from descendants of two of Hemings’s sons, Madison and Eston. (Of her other four children, two died in infancy, and the other two didn’t have any known offspring.) Not only did the researchers find that Madison’s and Eston’s descendants share Jefferson’s DNA; many of them had more of it than do his known descendants by way of his wife, Martha Wayles. [ Read: When slavery is erased from plantations ] For many Americans, the matter was already laid to rest years ago

In 1998, the scientific journal Nature published a two-page peer-reviewed paper titled “Jefferson Fathered Slave’s Last Child.” Newspaper stories declared the case solved, and Oprah Winfrey staged a tearful family reunion of Jefferson’s descendants
Most historians came to accept the finding when it was combined with other evidence from the era
But a vocal minority has continued to doubt that the two had a sexual relationship

Some have pointed out, correctly, that the limited biological data used in the Nature study did not definitively prove that Jefferson was the father of Hemings’s children—only that he was one of several candidates in the Jefferson male line
These doubters also disparage as unreliable or wishful thinking the oral histories passed down by Hemings’s descendants who have placed Jefferson in their family tree
Some detractors saw a more nefarious agenda

One researcher called the 1998 study “a deliberate attempt to select and mold the evidence to fit a pre-selected theory.” Other critics, many of them white Virginians, joined in the defense of the Founder. “Jefferson’s personal reputation has been all but assassinated,” wrote William G

Hyland Jr., a lawyer and author. “The face on Mount Rushmore has been vilified as a slave-owning hypocrite, misogynist, and racist.” Though the new results might convince some holdouts, the backlash has already arrived, and more will likely follow

The Heritage Foundation has previously criticized Monticello’s depiction of Jefferson in part for failing to tell visitors “that historians disagree about Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings.” The Thomas Jefferson Heritage Society, a nonprofit formed in response to the Nature report, still accuses “historical revisionists” of inaccurately portraying Jefferson as a “liar, fraud, hypocrite, and child molesting slave rapist.” The Trump administration has made clear that it wants to present a version of American history that doesn’t disparage the Founders

In a report released on the Fourth of July, the White House condemned what it asserted is “extreme political activism” guiding the 180-year-old Smithsonian, which President Trump has said is too focused on “how bad Slavery was.” For Clara Nutt, though, the results are simply confirmation of a long-known fact
Her African American father told his freckled daughter at an early age that she was a direct descendant of Jefferson through Madison Hemings
Nutt provided the researchers with saliva samples that found 5.1 percent of Jefferson’s genetic makeup in her DNA—nearly twice the amount expected by genetic averaging
She was delighted but not surprised to have scientific proof. “I have always known who I am,” Nutt told me
T hat the very person who made famous the phrase “All men are created equal” repeatedly impregnated a woman he held in lifetime bondage first surfaced in a Richmond newspaper in 1802
The writer, a Scottish-born journalist named James Callender, had once been a Jefferson champion, and had received financial support from him
But when Jefferson won the 1800 election, he denied a government job to the volatile Callender, who had been jailed during John Adams’s administration for sedition

Ally turned enemy. “By this wench Sally, our president has had several children,” Callender wrote in The Recorder . “The AFRICAN VENUS is said to officiate, as housekeeper at Monticello.” The Hemings-Jefferson matter became one of the nation’s first major political scandals—and one of its most enduring. “This engaged six of the seven first presidents,” Richard Kurin told me. “You could call it the longest-running American soap opera”—one, he notes, that involves the issues of race, inequality, and liberty

Jefferson, after all, declared in 1814 that “amalgamation with the other color produces a degradation to which no lover of his country, no lover of excellence in the human character can innocently consent.” By that date, his youngest child with Hemings, Eston, was 6 years old
Jefferson’s granddaughter Ellen Randolph Coolidge, in an 1858 letter to her husband, referred to the possibility of a relationship with Hemings as that which “will not bear telling
There are such things, after all, as moral impossibilities.” The Founder went to his grave without publicly acknowledging the relationship or any children he’d had with Hemings

A 1974 book by the historian Fawn Brodie reignited the debate with fresh historical evidence of Jefferson’s long-term liaison with Hemings, but Brodie’s assertions gained little traction among scholars and intellectuals

If the Hemings story was true, one skeptical historian wrote in 1977, then Jefferson “deserves to be regarded as one of the most profligate liars and consummate hypocrites ever to occupy the presidency.” Gore Vidal summarized the prevailing sentiment in an interview: “No gentleman would have gone to bed with a slave
Since Thomas Jefferson was the greatest gentleman of his period, he could not have done so either

That takes care of that.” Two decades later, the Harvard law professor Annette Gordon-Reed sharply criticized the academic community for spending “generations either ignoring or explaining away” the nearly four-decade relationship and accepting white narratives denying the tie while dismissing those left by Black families that asserted otherwise
The 1998 Nature report brought the new tools of genetics to bear on the dispute
The authors based their biological data on the Y chromosome, passed down by Jefferson’s male descendants

But some researchers accused the authors of misleading the public, and the authors were forced to acknowledge that Jefferson could “neither be definitively excluded nor solely implicated” by their data
Other candidates included his younger brother, Randolph, a frequent visitor to Monticello

One enslaved informant had called Randolph “a mighty simple man” who “used to come out among black people, play the fiddle & dance half the night.” A month after the Nature study’s publication, the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which owns and operates Monticello, convened a group of scholars to examine the genetic and historical data

A 2000 statistical analysis by a Monticello archaeologist strengthened the case made in Nature by examining the timing of when Jefferson was present at Monticello and when Hemings’s children were conceived
A majority of the foundation’s panel found “a high probability” that at least one of Hemings’s children had been fathered by Jefferson, and likely all six

title: The Michael Kelly Award from The Atlantic is Awarded to Drew Philp for “There Will Be No Mercy” published in The Atavist Magazine
excerpt: Drew Philp is the winner of the 23rd annual Michael Kelly Award, given by The Atlantic , for his investigative feature “ There Will Be No Mercy ,” published by
body: Drew Philp is the winner of the 23rd annual Michael Kelly Award, given by The Atlantic , for his investigative feature “ There Will Be No Mercy ,” published by The Atavist Magazine in 2025
Philp’s harrowing exposé of Ethiopia’s civil war serves as the definitive account of the two-year conflict, considered one of the deadliest of this century
The award was announced this morning at The Atlantic Festival in New York City

Philp’s article recounted the conflict in Ethiopia through the lens of a single hospital, suddenly overwhelmed with casualties as government soldiers targeted not only combatants but civilians, including children, in the province of Tigray
Philp followed doctors such as Abraha Gebreegziabher, a pediatrician, who confronted the carnage in the hospital even as he wondered why powerful nations simply stood by
In his acceptance speech today, Philp said: “Across the world, people are watching the West break its promises and squander nearly a century of goodwill
Abraha, are beginning to look elsewhere for hope and the rule of law
This is a failure that threatens to topple all of our successes

When we in the West abandon the law and commitment to dignity, when we allow international institutions to be corrupted, when we stand idle as our allies commit atrocities—even genocide—and yes, when we commit atrocities ourselves, we corrupt our own democracy and bomb our own credibility abroad and at home.” The Michael Kelly Award judges praised the clarity and poignancy of Philp’s writing and the depth of his reporting on the suffering of the Tigrayan people at the hands of the Ethiopian government. “There Will Be No Mercy” won a National Magazine Award for reporting and a citation for excellence from the Overseas Press Club of America’s Madeline Dane Ross Award

Presented annually by The Atlantic , the Michael Kelly Award honors journalists whose work exemplifies “the fearless pursuit and expression of truth,” which defined Michael Kelly’s own life and career
Kelly was the first journalist killed in the course of the Iraq War, in 2003
He served as editor of The Atlantic and National Journal when both magazines were publications of Atlantic Media, chaired by David G
Bradley created the award in Kelly’s honor

Journalists from three other news organizations were recognized as finalists: Elliott Woods, at Texas Monthly , for his two-part account of the worst immigration disaster in American history; Emily Baumgaertner Nunn of The New York Times Magazine , for her feature on sex trafficking in Los Angeles; and Elizabeth Weil, at New York magazine’s The Cut , for her moving stories on sibling sexual abuse and nonverbal autistic children

Five judges selected the winner and the finalists: Ena Alvarado, a writer and former assistant editor at The Atlantic ; Charles Green, a former editor of National Journal ; Adam Harris, a staff writer at The Atlantic ; Cullen Murphy, an editor at large of The Atlantic ; and Sarah Topol, now a staff writer at The Atlantic and a past winner of the Michael Kelly Award
More information about Michael Kelly and the award in his honor can be found at theatlantic.com/michael-kelly-award
Press Contacts: Anna Bross and Sammi Sontag | The Atlantic press@theatlantic.com

title: What the Kennedy Center’s Tax Return Reveals
excerpt: For 19 months, Donald Trump has portrayed himself as the Kennedy Center’s savior
body: For 19 months, Donald Trump has portrayed himself as the Kennedy Center’s savior
He promised to root out “woke” programming at the arts complex
He claimed that past leaders had neglected dangerous conditions in the building—a structure that he now says might have to be “ripped down” if he can’t put his name on it
Throughout his tenure, he and his allies have accused former executives of financial mismanagement and even “fraud” that left the organization struggling
Now there’s a fuller picture of the finances Trump inherited—and of what happened during his first months in charge

A previously unseen federal tax filing captures an institution in transition: It spans the final months of its previous leadership and roughly seven months under Trump, offering a baseline for understanding a financial crisis that has grown more severe over the year that has followed. (The Kennedy Center provided me with the filing because nonprofits are required to do so within 30 days of a request.) On paper, the Kennedy Center had an extraordinary financial year
It reported more than $516 million in total revenue on its 990 form for the fiscal year that began in October 2024 and ended last September—a nearly $210 million increase from the previous year

But that windfall appears to have been largely driven by a summer infusion of federal renovation money, which Trump had asked Congress to include in its One Big Beautiful Bill Act and is now threatening to withhold

If you subtract the $257 million in renovation funds from the revenue, the Kennedy Center appears to have spent nearly $47 million more than it took in that fiscal year, a precipitous drop compared with the funds reported on its previous 990
Notably, the new filing includes a $48 million “bad debt expense,” which is essentially a write-down of previously recorded revenue that an organization no longer expects to collect

In the fiscal year ending in 2024, when the center was led by President Deborah Rutter and a bipartisan board of trustees, it brought in about $40 million more than it spent. (The Kennedy Center and the White House did not immediately respond to questions about the return.) Stripping out the renovation money does not necessarily mean the Kennedy Center ran a $47 million deficit last fiscal year
Two experts I spoke with cautioned that the tax return does not provide enough information to make that calculation cleanly

One of them, Michael Kaiser, an arts-management consultant and a former Kennedy Center president, told me that 990s combine operating revenue and expenses with capital funding and other sources of income, making it difficult to isolate the institution’s underlying financial performance from top-line figures. “It combines everything into one mush,” he said
The other expert, Cleopatra Charles, a Rutgers University professor whose research focuses on nonprofit organizations and financial management, reached a similar conclusion

Taken at face value, she told me, the filing depicts a “very financially healthy organization.” Total revenue increased by roughly 68 percent, and contributions and grants more than doubled, allowing the center to report that $210 million surplus
But much of that apparent improvement came from a one-off appropriation rather than the Kennedy Center’s own programming or fundraising efforts

The form noted $301.5 million in federal appropriations—a figure that includes both the money from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the roughly $45 million in annual funding the center typically receives
The tax filing bolsters what reporting (and rows of empty seats at performances) over the past year and a half has shown
Program-service revenue, a category that includes ticket sales and other income generated by programming, fell from nearly $105 million the previous year to about $89 million
Kaiser cautioned that this figure can fluctuate considerably depending on the mix of productions
A blockbuster musical such as Hamilton , for instance, could bring a significant bump in ticket revenue that disappears the following year
Other figures on the return raise more questions than answers
There was an unusual increase in net income from unrelated business activities, which rose from about $27,000 in 2023–24 to more than $517,000 in the latest year reported
But the filing does not make clear what generated this increase

Charles pointed out a roughly $43 million increase in “other expenses” that lacked a clear explanation of what they were—including nearly $35 million categorized as “other contracted services.” Taken together, she said, the line items lacked sufficient context about the center’s finances—and an independent audit would offer more clarity
But according to the 990 form, the annual audit was not completed by the time of filing
That’s “very unusual,” a former official with knowledge of Kennedy Center governance and financial practices told me, speaking on the condition of anonymity out of fear of professional repercussions
Audits are usually made available to the public by January or February each year
The Kennedy Center that Trump took over was still recovering from the pandemic, during which it shut down entirely; it did not reopen fully until fall 2021
The center posted deficits during the pandemic but had surpluses in the two years before the Trump takeover
It draws revenue from ticket sales, charitable giving, government funding, campus rentals, and other sources
Trump’s putsch disrupted several of those streams: Many artists canceled performances, a segment of the audience began to boycott the center, and some donors pulled back on contributions
That included perhaps the center’s most important benefactor in recent years
To become the Kennedy Center’s chairman, Trump ousted the private-equity billionaire David Rubenstein , who had donated more than $100 million to the organization

By last fall, ticket sales to classical-music and theater performances were in free fall and the center had taken on a more political flavor, hosting evangelical-Christian and conservative events as well as the World Cup draw, where Trump received the FIFA Peace Prize
But it’s unclear if the Kennedy Center was able to make up the ground it had lost in ticket sales by attracting more donors

The Washington Post reported last month that ticket sales and donations had plunged even further after last December, when a board largely composed of Trump allies voted to rename the Kennedy Center to honor the current president

The ongoing legal battle over the future of the organization centers on two issues: the appropriateness of that board’s decision this March to shut down for the renovation, and whether Trump’s name can be added to a “living memorial” to a slain president
Center officials recently warned that the organization was nearing bankruptcy —confirming many observers’ suspicions

The board wants Trump’s help to raise the necessary funds, and to recognize his efforts by inscribing his name on the building, which a federal judge has rejected several times, saying Congress did not permit such a change when it established the venue

title: The Rise of Parasite Authors
excerpt: Editor’s note: This work is part of AI Watchdog , The Atlantic ’s ongoing investigation into the generative-AI industry
body: Editor’s note: This work is part of AI Watchdog , The Atlantic ’s ongoing investigation into the generative-AI industry
Earlier this summer, Tamra Westberry received a Facebook notification that made her heart sink
A fellow author had taken to social media to endorse Westberry’s latest book, Project Erebus , after reading about it in a weekly roundup of the latest paranormal-romance releases
Independent authors like Westberry, who is based in Texas and has published dozens of books under the pen name Tara West, usually welcome an encouraging word and a bit of cross-promotion
She had never heard of a book called Project Erebus
She looked up her author profile on Amazon, and there it was: Project Erebus , a book that featured character names she’d previously used, with a cover echoing that of her recent work
Translations were available in German, French, Italian, and Spanish

The book was a complete mystery to her, but after she read its sample pages, she suspected it was made by someone who’d used AI tools. (I ran the book’s cover and promotional blurb through Pangram, which suggested that they were completely AI-generated.) Westberry emailed Amazon and requested that the company delink the unaffiliated books from her profile
Amazon removed the books from the platform within a week or so—but not before some of her fans purchased them, read them, and left reviews. “No real detail, characters remain undeveloped

I almost felt I was reading an essay written by a school child,” one disappointed reader wrote in a two-star review for Project Erebus on Goodreads, a literary social network owned by Amazon that had also attributed the book to West. [ Read: These 183,000 Books Are Fueling The Biggest Fight In Publishing And Tech ] Across categories—fantasy, horror, even coloring books—writers say they’re seeing AI-generated listings crop up on their Amazon author pages

Some of these works are in entirely different genres from their usual work—such as a children’s series misattributed to a writer of steamy love stories—whereas others echo the subject matter or jacket designs of preexisting books
One writer reported someone sneaking in a fake edition under the listing of their real book
Because Amazon often sends out emails notifying author-page followers about new listings, these titles are able to leech a writer’s fan base, make ill-gotten revenue, and confuse readers
AI companies pirated millions of books to train today’s most popular models, as The Atlantic has previously reported
Those models are now being used to churn out books in a matter of minutes and place them alongside books that represent years of hard work
In some cases, people go beyond mass-producing second-rate content or publishing copycats of new releases, using the names of established authors on parasitic works that feed off preexisting brands

Writers feel that they have little recourse regarding what AI models ingest, or spit out. “It’s deeply unsettling, after I spent years crafting stories and building my brand, that some no-talent grifter can bottom-feed off my fan base with AI slop,” Westberry, who’s written more than 50 books that were included in a data set used by the likes of OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic, told me
The parasite-creator problem is pervasive
Professors have found AI-generated academic papers published under their names; recent reporting suggests that sneaking AI-generated songs onto artists’ streaming profiles is a relatively simple move
The issue has also become endemic to Amazon, the world’s largest online book retailer, which sells hundreds of millions of books annually in the U.S. alone
The platform groups works with the same byline under a unified profile thanks to a largely automatic system
Authors say that Amazon has failed to make a concerted effort to address the phenomenon, and that the onus falls on them to monitor their pages, in a crazy-making game of whack-a-mole

An Amazon spokesperson told me that the company does take measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates its guidelines, but it did not provide more details about how these systems work. “We are committed to a bookstore that readers love and publishers and authors trust, and work directly with authors to address any issues or errors affecting their accounts,” the spokesperson said
To some degree, Amazon’s parasite-author problem predates the widespread advent of AI
A decade ago, Stephen King publicly urged the site to stop associating his own works with those of Stephen R
King., another horror author whose name was confusing fans
Such instances, however, were few and far between because of the time and effort it required to publish a title
Now that anyone can use LLMs to churn out a novel, the issue has both grown and mutated

While the sheer number of new books published on the platform might inevitably lead to more authors of the same name, Orna Ross, the founder of the Alliance of Independent Authors, noted that many titles are purposefully designed to blend in with a real author’s catalog. “It needs only to fool the algorithm and a rushed buyer for long enough to skim the sale,” she told me
Authors told me that Amazon is typically quick to delink books from author pages once they’ve been flagged
But getting them removed from the platform entirely can be trickier, especially if a writer hasn’t trademarked their name
Amazon can treat such incidents as a matter of “name coincidence,” Ross said, and leave books up even after decoupling them from profiles

Writers struggling to receive direct action from Amazon have also escalated cases through the Authors Guild, the largest professional organization for writers in America, whose recent reports have warned of AI books falsely attributed to writers
For many writers of genre fiction, which relies on high output and familiar tropes, staying afloat means playing a volume game, releasing numerous books a year to make a living
That makes certain genres particularly susceptible to AI dupes, which can blend in with the thousands of real titles released annually

Because producing AI versions is so cheap, even a few sales can be profitable. “The people that are making money selling AI copies are generally doing so by selling one or two or three copies of the thousand different books that they publish,” Julie Trelstad, a publishing consultant, told me
The identity of the individuals behind these books is a mystery to real authors, and often difficult to track down
Regardless, authors don’t view such books as a major sales threat, given that they tend to be less appealing to buyers than genuine works, with slapdash covers and lackluster page counts

What writers are really concerned about is the potential for long-lasting reputational harm among readers, who typically trust that a book listed on an Amazon author page was, indeed, written by said author
Last year, Vanessa O’Loughlin, an Irish author who writes crime books under the name Sam Blake, was alerted to a trilogy of “dark romantasy” books on her profile that she suspected were made with AI

title: The Goal of Contemporary Journalism
excerpt: In a conversation at The Atlantic Festival, Jeffrey Goldberg, The Atlantic ’s editor in chief, spoke with Amna Nawaz, a co-anchor and co-managing editor of PBS
body: In a conversation at The Atlantic Festival, Jeffrey Goldberg, The Atlantic ’s editor in chief, spoke with Amna Nawaz, a co-anchor and co-managing editor of PBS NewsHour , and Joe Kahn, the executive editor of The New York Times , about the state of independent media
In his second term, Donald Trump has escalated his confrontations with the press

The New York Times was personally sued by Trump for $15 billion and, separately, the paper’s journalists were recently served subpoenas for reporting on the Qatari jet gifted to the White House. (The Department of Justice subsequently withdrew these subpoenas.) Federal support for PBS was scrapped last year
And as self-styled journalists proliferate online, public trust in the media is at record lows

Evan Smith, the panel’s moderator and The Atlantic ’s managing director for events, referred to the guests as outliers for having weathered these attacks—“You’ve survived.” Nawaz responded, “I wouldn’t put it in the past tense

We are surviving .” With so many “content creators” and pundits now claiming to be journalists, Goldberg reflected on how the internet has changed the journalism industry. “There was this view for a while—in the last 20 years—that the democratization of media was an unadulterated good thing,” he noted
Indeed, for decades, the media was “too stringent about who gets to talk.” But with that shift, “standards were lowered

Standards for what counts as actual verified information.” Public distrust in the media, and the president’s frequent attacks on reporters and their employers, have made the work of journalism more difficult. “I remember, back in 2017, boarding a plane with my then-4-year-old daughter, and the man ahead of us was wearing a T-shirt that said in block letters on the back: Journalist

To restore public faith, the panelists agreed that journalists need to be transparent about the work that they do. “The further that news and information travels away from the individual human-being journalists who do the work, the less trust there is,” Kahn said. “Original reporting is still by far the most valuable thing.” He later added: “Kind of objectively, I think we’re killing it.” The following conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity
Evan Smith: What is the job of journalism today? Jeff, we talked about this when you were on my PBS show a few months ago
Here’s what you said: “The goal of any quality journalism operation these days is to put as much truth into the universe as possible.” Say more about that, please
Jeffrey Goldberg: I continue to agree with what I said to you on your show
There’s two levels of your question, “What do editors in chief do?,” and mostly what we do is keep things moving
Try to go deep on the problems that exist day to day
The last 11 years have helped us focus on core tasks
We thought most questions were settled: The First Amendment is the First Amendment; the freedom of the press is vitally important; the media plays an indispensable role in any democracy
That’s bad for civilization, that they’re under pressure and that these questions are unsettled
It’s good for us in the sense that it helps clarify the purpose
So you wake up every morning with even more of a sense of mission than maybe you would in ordinary times
I always tell our staff this, and I’m borrowing from Marty Baron, the former editor of The Washington Post : We’re not going to war
And as long as you just remember that your job every day is to find out something that’s true, contextualize it, treat it fairly, and write it accurately, that’s great
You finished the day by putting something out there
You hope that it elevates the ideology of truth
It’s sad that these concepts are under pressure
I can only speak for myself, but it’s great to wake up with that purpose
Conspiracy theories and misinformation are running rampant
It is harder than ever to meet the Goldberg standard, isn’t it? Joe Kahn: It is
And the task for us is to do, as Jeffrey said, to wake up every day, to do original reporting
Ideally, bring new information to light on all the stories that matter every day, and to get it out there, increasingly in forms that people want to consume that information
And that mission is under stress, but it’s more critical than ever
And it makes the job even more vital to American democracy than it ever was
And I would really emphasize the original reporting and new information
We’re in an environment where people feel like they can get information in their feeds nonstop, 24 hours a day

They’re hearing it in their AirPods, but actual new original reporting that relies on expert reporters who are going to the scene of news, who are asking tough questions, is in short supply, and it’s on us to find a way to get that to more people
Smith: Amna, the stakes could not be higher in this extraordinary moment
Or, at least, that’s what we all keep saying over and over
Informed communities strengthen democracy
And in a democracy, an informed electorate is what powers our democracy
I couldn’t agree more with everything that Joe and Jeff just said
I look at it as the advice I got from my very first boss in journalism

title: Lina Khan on Doomer Panic and Ending AI Exceptionalism
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube As “rogue” AI agents hack systems and leaders warn of catastrophe, who should be held responsible? Former FTC
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube As “rogue” AI agents hack systems and leaders warn of catastrophe, who should be held responsible? Former FTC Commissioner Lina Khan argues that the United States already has a lot of the regulatory tools needed

In this live episode from The Atlantic Festival, the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Khan about why the AI-alarmism conversation feels a little off, how money affects politics and regulation, and some of the ways she would be dealing with AI if she were still the head of the FTC
The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel
And this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna talk about what on earth to do about the AI companies who are saying their products might kill us all
And I’ve got quite literally the perfect person to talk about this with, the chair of New York City’s Economic Development Corporation and the former chair of the FTC under Joe Biden, Lina Khan

A bit more than a week ago, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, quit his job and he published a warning: The AI companies, he argued, were not taking safety seriously and they were, quote, “gambling with our lives.” The product that he’d spent the past three years working on was spiraling out of the control of the people who were building it, and it might someday, he said, end humanity
His warning echoed what AI executives, researchers, effective altruists on forums, and Bay Area doomers have been anxiously posting about and writing best-selling books about for more than a decade
But Coxon’s warning did what all those other warnings failed to do
It broke containment, and it created a national conversation

Concerned lawmakers called for emergency AI meetings; President Obama weighed in; Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk all came to a rare consensus and called for a slowdown of AI development
President Donald Trump responded to all of it by calling AI fears “a hoax.” Things are moving fast
But one thing is clear: The AI-safety conversation is happening at a global scale among insiders and normies alike

And there are almost unending questions here: How real is this threat? Is this hype and AI-company marketing? But no matter where you land on the actual risk of these companies, there is a question about what we should do about it
The companies themselves are calling for a regulatory framework, including independent auditors of the models

Is all of this progress, or are the tech companies simply trying to get favorable, cushy terms that lock them into virtual monopolies? In other words, is all of their talk earnest, or is this a power grab? What should AI-company regulation look like? Why is nobody holding these companies accountable right now? Do we need new laws? Or should we be using the existing ones better? What are the historical parallels here? Are we in uncharted waters, or is this a normal crisis that is playing out at abnormal speed and abnormal scale? Lina Khan has spent her career wrestling with a lot of these questions, specifically as they apply to Silicon Valley’s tech giants
As FTC chair, she was part of a genuine shift in antitrust enforcement, arguing that traditional U.S. competition laws were broken and ill-suited for digital platforms

Now, late last week, as the AI debate was roiling, Khan posted on X that the AI regulation needed to take into account that “law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products.” So what does enforcement look like in this AI moment? Where do we go from here? I spoke with Lina Khan on Thursday morning in New York at The Atlantic Festival
Here’s our conversation. [ Music ] Warzel: Thank you all for coming

And I wanted to start with the news that has been all-consuming in the tech and political spheres over the last week or so, which is the AI-research whistleblowers warning of AI agents spinning out of control that might “kill us all.” Calls from Sam Altman, Dario [Amodei], Elon Musk, others to slow down development, quote “pace the frontier.” You weighed in on the regulatory angle on X recently

But first I just wanted to ask, why do you think this safety panic is breaking through now? Khan: Well, I think we’ve been seeing it for the last few years, you know, various predictions about what may happen with these tools

And it certainly seems like there have been various inflection points where people within these companies have seen what they would describe potentially as a step change in terms of certain capabilities
It seems like most recently, there have been more instances of agents basically becoming more overtly defective
Some people may call them rogue, really exceeding the parameters of what people and humans had set up them to do
And so that seems to be the latest catalyst

But I think there’s been, you know, a drumbeat in the background now for several years, including when I was back at the FTC, when we were already starting to confront less these existential questions around, you know, Could we see the eradication of humanity? and more of the bread and butter of How are these tools already impacting people in their day-to-day? I mean, for most Americans, the way they interact with AI is through a chatbot and trying to get customer service, and instead being stuck in some doom loop
Right? So I think there are a lot of ways that this is manifesting, and I think the regulatory-policy conversation can happen across that spectrum

Warzel: Some of the concern, I think, too, comes from this idea that the models that these companies have trained and, you know, that power a lot of these chatbots, they are themselves very—they’re part of this black box
Right? Like, we don’t really know exactly what’s going into them with the weights, with the training, all of that

When you were at the FTC, when this was all kind of very young and new, what kind of sense did you get about that level of transparency and what we can’t see? Khan: I mean, there’s a tremendous amount that we can’t see, which is not unique in terms of, you know, the relationship between an enforcer or regulator and a company, but certainly seems to be even more acute in this context
But, you know, we were already encountering black-box algorithms

And what does an enforcer do when it’s really an algorithm that is, you know, resulting in various types of products being shown or not being shown? And what does that mean for our existing laws? I do think one pattern that we’ve seen across various moments when a new technology hits is that there can be this rush to create some exceptionalism around it, especially vis-à-vis the existing laws and regulations
And so one thing that was very important to me when I was serving in government was to make very clear that there was not any AI exemption from existing laws on the books
And I think we see, even now, a strain in the conversation around new regulation that seems to assume that these current developments are happening in some legal vacuum

Like, you know, if you’re working on one of these companies, you still have an existing obligation to abide by, you know, consumer-protection laws, antidiscrimination laws, antitrust laws, product-liability regimes
And so part of what I’ve tried to, you know, include in the conversation is this realization that we may want to talk about new rules and regulations
But let’s not forget that existing legal obligations absolutely apply
And some of what we’re hearing from these firms and their executives suggests that the legal care that is already required of these firms is not being taken

Warzel: Why do you think that everyone in the industry is behaving—and even, you know, some politicians are behaving—like these companies are exempt? What is the reason for that? Khan: It’s a great question
I mean, I think part of it absolutely stems back to how the firms themselves market their capabilities
And when there is a push for regulation—I mean, we’ve seen this even in, you know, context around crypto, where there was a push to say, Well, existing security laws don’t apply

title: Could AI really kill us all? Your questions, answered.
excerpt: The jury is out on the most apocalyptic scenarios
body: The jury is out on the most apocalyptic scenarios

AI-powered drones and cyberattacks on hospitals are dangerous, and bioweapons designed with AI assistance are a real near-term threat—but AI wiping out humanity is still science fiction territory for now
Alignment is the field trying to prevent the worst outcomes

Researchers are working to ensure AI does what we want and nothing more, but even the best-resourced labs haven't cracked it—models remain unpredictable and can pursue goals in unsanctioned ways when pushed
Regulating AI is hard when we barely understand it
Monitoring tools are fragile, AI companies have obvious conflicts of interest in policing themselves, and the US government has so far declined to step in meaningfully
All this doom talk could actually shape future AI behavior

LLMs learn from what they read, including articles like this one—meaning today's apocalyptic discourse could subtly prime tomorrow's models toward exactly the scenarios we're worried about. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144435" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> On Wednesday, MIT Technology Review hosted a live Roundtables event for subscribers that asked the question everyone’s asking right now: Could AI really kill us all? But attendees had so many more questions than we had time to answer in the 30 minute session
So we asked our senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins to round up some of the best questions attendees submitted and try their best to answer them
Thanks to all who submitted questions! Am I gonna die? Yes, eventually
Unfortunately, my journalistic powers of prognostication aren’t powerful enough for me to tell you how
AI-powered drones have already killed people in Ukraine, and AI-driven cyberattacks on hospitals will surely claim victims before long.  Could AI go even further, and kill all of us? Less likely
But some people—quirky people, but undeniably knowledgeable about AI—have been warning for years that this could happen

And while I’m not yet stockpiling canned food or trying to get in good with a bunker-owning megabillionaire, I have noticed that the doomers’ predictions about AI capabilities and alignment have, over the past couple of years, proved disconcertingly accurate

That certainly doesn’t mean that their more dire forecasts will come true, but it’s enough for me to sit up and take notice. — Grace Huckins Are you going to die because of AI? I’d say there’s a non-zero chance
Let’s say you’re unlucky enough to be the victim of a freakish near-future event or accident
Maybe it’s a cyberattack carried out by a swarm of AI agents on critical infrastructure
Sadly, a scenario like that now no longer feels as far-fetched as it once did
Or maybe a novel AI-designed pathogen cuts through the population
Or the world economy crashes, causing conflicts and famine
Both plausible, but I think less likely.  Are we all going to die because of AI? Nope
There are no circumstances outside of apocalyptic science fiction in which AI could kill us all
You can spin up any number of scare stories, but they’re not grounded in present-day realities about what the tech can do or where it’s headed
Some people argue that there’s no harm in preparing for the worst, however wacky it might seem

But I think such catastrophizing can make people excuse or overlook many of the more immediate problems with the existing technology and the companies building it. — Will Douglas Heaven Why would AI kill us? Someone might tell it to, and it might listen

That’s part of the reason researchers are so concerned about AI’s biological capabilities—imagine what Aum Shinrikyo, the doomsday cult behind the Tokyo subway sarin attack of 1995, would have done with a tool that could design a pathogen deadlier than Ebola and more transmissible than measles
Those of us who don’t want to die have to figure out how to defend against all plausible biological weapons, but our would-be attackers only have to manufacture one effective pathogen
Then there’s the more exotic-sounding possibility that an AI could decide to kill us itself

There are various stories about how this might happen out there, but the most widespread involve AI systems that don’t hate people, necessarily—we are just an obstacle between them and the goals that we gave them

Much as the OpenAI agents behind the Hugging Face hack compromised another site’s infrastructure to get a good score on a test, the idea is that some future, more powerful AI might get rid of us to prevent us from shutting it down—all in pursuit of some goal that we instructed it to go after.  — Grace Huckins How can we best ensure alignment so the worst doesn ’ t happen, and who is doing the best work to achieve it? Alignment is a huge area of research
In simple terms, it involves building models that behave in ways we want them to and not in ways we don’t
We need to trust agents better before handing over more autonomy
Alignment is supposed to establish that trust
LLMs aren’t designed in the way other software is, where dos and don’ts can be hard-coded in
Instead, aligned behavior needs to be instilled when models are trained
One approach is to reward them for doing things you want them to (a little like raising a toddler, perhaps)
Another approach involves giving an LLM a written list of rules it is supposed to follow (kind of like a constitution)
Anthropic and OpenAI are both leaders in this field—and yet neither has been able to develop models that are fully aligned
A big problem is that LLMs are far more inconsistent and far less predictable than people
They can behave in one way in one situation and another way in a situation that to us seems very similar

title: The specter of AI-enabled bioweapons is a wake-up call for biotech
excerpt: AI could make bioweapons disturbingly easy to build: In 2022, researchers accidentally generated 40,000 potential chemical warfare agents in under six hours usi
body: AI could make bioweapons disturbingly easy to build: In 2022, researchers accidentally generated 40,000 potential chemical warfare agents in under six hours using a drug-discovery AI — some more toxic than known nerve agents

Existing safeguards have real limits: Anthropic recently confirmed users had tried exploiting its models to make viruses more transmissible and dangerous, highlighting an ongoing cat-and-mouse game between protections and workarounds

Scientists disagree on how worried to be: Some biologists argue AI tools aren't yet capable enough to fully develop bioweapons, while others warn that a determined actor would "eventually succeed" — and urge preparing now. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144329" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In recent weeks, leaders of some of the biggest AI companies have warned that the very tech they are developing is dangerous
Last weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that AI carries serious risk and that progress should be slowed

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded on X : “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” Those posts came a few days after the AI researcher Jacob Coxon announced that he was leaving a role at Anthropic, charging that neither it nor OpenAI (where he had also worked) was acting responsibly. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he posted on X

Another Anthropic employee, Evan Hubinger, publicly agreed with him. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he responded on X . “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” One of the ways they fear AI might end us all is by somehow aiding the design, creation, and release of some kind of bioweapon
A bioweapon might be a highly lethal virus that targets people according to their genes
It could be a fungus that wipes out a crop and causes food insecurity
Perhaps it would be a tasteless, odorless toxin that could be slipped into a region’s water supply, undetected
The concern is that AI tools can be used to help generate agents like these
In 2022, researchers at Collaborations Pharmaceuticals found that it was remarkably easy to do so using an AI “molecule generator” they’d developed to find potential drugs for human disease
In less than six hours, the model generated 40,000 molecules with the potential to serve as chemical warfare agents

Some of them were designed to be even more toxic than known nerve agents. “Without being overly alarmist, this should serve as a wake-up call for our colleagues in the ‘AI in drug discovery’ community,” the authors wrote at the time

It was a wake-up call for David Magnus, a professor of medicine and biomedical ethics at Stanford University, even though he had been assessing the risks associated with the misuse of medical science and biotechnology since the late 1990s. “That was very scary to me,” he says. “Of course, everything since then has just sort of blown up.” Today, AI bots can answer questions on topics spanning all realms of science

Anyone can use large language models trained on the knowledge and experience of “almost every scientist who ever lived on this planet,” says Dunja Sabra, a biosecurity researcher at the University of Hamburg in Germany
Those models can provide instructions and video training on how to conduct experiments

Combine that with advances in biotech that have made gene editing and synthetic biology tools much more accessible (the “DIY biology” movement has already enabled many people to set up labs at home), and you’ve got a potentially very dangerous situation. “The chances are that someone determined would succeed eventually,” Sabra says
People who want to build new genomes must typically order the pieces of DNA from companies that screen for suspicious requests

Responsible researchers put potentially risky research through rounds of analysis called “red-teaming,” in which independent scientists look for ways the work might be misused, and “blue-teaming,” where others come up with potential mitigations
And AI companies have tweaked their tools in attempts to prevent them from offering up scientific information that could be misused
But none of these protections are ironclad

In a report published last week, Anthropic acknowledged that people had attempted to use its models to explore ways to make the chikungunya virus more transmissible, create a form of bird flu that is more dangerous to humans, and build an “atlas of venom toxin peptides,” among other things. “We’ve got a constant back and forth,” says Magnus. “We have to build better surveillance and screening tools, [but] AI is really good at figuring out ways around them.” We’ll probably need to use AI to find ways to restrict the use of AI, he says
I should add here that not all scientists agree on the level of risk

At a recent media briefing, some biologists at Imperial College London argued that AI tools just aren’t good enough to fully develop bioweapons, and that testing new pathogens requires difficult, time-consuming, human work
Some think the guardrails we have in place are sufficient

And Wendy Barclay, a professor of infectious disease at Imperial, pointed out that, as things stand, the greatest risk of a pandemic isn’t from a bioweapon, but from pathogens that are already circulating
Take H5N1, the bird flu virus that has already killed millions of birds and spread widely through US dairy cattle; last month it was also detected in captive mink at a farm in Utah
Sabra, on the other hand, likes to think five to 10 years ahead

Countries should be strengthening their health-care systems, preparing antidotes to known toxins, and stockpiling medicines, she says: “We need to be prepared.” Kevin Esvelt, an MIT biologist who invented both technology to fast-track the propagation of a genetic feature through an entire population and ways to limit that technology, echoed these concerns in an X post on Wednesday, stating that a large language model had “disclosed a novel form of bioweapon that I hadn’t realized was possible.” He added, “Please, for the love of God, children, the future of humanity, or whatever you consider holy, let’s err on the side of caution here.” This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter

title: Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood
url:
<title>Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Annie Dillard is rightly celebrated as a <a href="https://apnews.com/article/annie-dillard-dies-pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-308e76e2beaffdd5836183a7a65bb6d3">pioneer in creative nonfiction</a> after her death on <a href="https://apnews.com/article/annie-dillard-dies-pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-308e76e2beaffdd5836183a7a65bb6d3">Sep. 15, 2026, at age 81</a>. But the dazzling, disorienting feel of Dillard’s work might be best understood as the often overlooked influence of poetry on her prose. </p>

<p>Dillard published her first full-length work of creative nonfiction, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-annie-dillard?variant=41232036790306">Pilgrim at Tinker Creek</a>,” when she was only 28. Winning her the <a href="https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/annie-dillard">1975 Pulitzer Prize</a>, this early book set the tone for her later work in creative nonfiction: the essay collection “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/teaching-a-stone-to-talk-annie-dillard?variant=41224300363810">Teaching a Stone to Talk</a>,” and full-length works “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/holy-the-firm-annie-dillard">Holy the Firm</a>” and “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/40917/for-the-time-being-by-annie-dillard/">For the Time Being</a>.” They all attend closely to the natural world, with a theologian’s eye and a poet’s idiom. </p>

<p>Dillard’s creative nonfiction about nature owes a debt to the lyrical prose of <a href="https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/transcendentalism/">transcendentalists</a> like <a href="https://theconversation.com/thoreau-the-scientist-how-environmental-research-informed-walden-and-later-works-281097">Henry David Thoreau</a>, whom Dillard cited as a major influence in her work. She was also overt about the central role that fiction played in her thinking in her book of literary criticism, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/living-by-fiction-annie-dillard?variant=41224700788770">Living by Fiction</a>.” </p>

<p>But Dillard’s nonfiction, though undeniably prose, can have “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/books/annie-dillard-dead.html">the shape and intensity of a poem</a>,” as her New York Times obituary puts it. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/profile/amy-cannon/">writer and writing professor</a>, I think often about how blurred the boundary between poetry and prose really is. Annie Dillard’s work embodies this permeability.</p>

<h2>Prose and poetry, in combination</h2>

<p>Not all writing is the same. Prose typically features continuous sentences arranged in paragraphs. <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315688374">Poetry tends to be differentiated from prose</a> by a deliberate organization of language that’s not determined by the page itself.  </p>

<p>Prose poetry, the lyric essay and other hybrid forms of literature play at the <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315666327">intersection of genre</a>, which usually defines these separate categories of writing. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511803024.008">Creative nonfiction</a> likewise aims to accurately convey reality while emphasizing literary style. The <a href="https://creativenonfiction.org/writing/the-5-rs-of-creative-nonfiction">literary features of creative nonfiction</a> are often drawn from fiction, with devices such as dialogue, scene and flashback. </p>

<p>But one of the distinctions of Annie Dillard’s nonfiction is how much her prose owes to poetry. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of Annie Dillard's 'The Writing Life,' held by Celeste Ng" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760824/original/file-20260918-50-mtf5rm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Annie Dillard’s attention to craft inspired many writers, including novelist Celeste Ng, who holds a copy of Dillard’s reflections in her personal library.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/celeste-ng-holds-her-copy-of-the-writing-life-by-annie-news-photo/2295097090">Sophie Park/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Poetry can be <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt2tt8jz">defined in many ways</a>, but it tends to be characterized by honed, heightened language. Poems are often noted for their memorable images, rich sounds and foregrounding of emotion. Dillard’s nonfiction is shot through with images that arrest readers with their beauty or confront readers with their terror – as in her Harper’s essay “<a href="https://harpers.org/archive/1976/05/the-death-of-a-moth/">The Death of a Moth</a>,” where the insect is drawn to a candle flame, becomes stuck in the wax and is transformed into a burning wick. In Dillard’s words:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>“She burned for two hours without changing, without swaying or kneeling – only glowing within, like a building fire glimpsed through silhouetted walls, like a hollow saint, like a flame-faced virgin gone to God, while I read by her light, kindled, while Rimbaud in Paris burnt out his brain in a thousand poems, while night pooled wetly at my feet.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>It’s no accident that Dillard describes herself as reading the work of French poet Arthur Rimbaud by the light of the moth. She previously wrote that she <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/40257790">loved how language sounds in French symbolist poetry</a>, and Rimbaud was known to <a href="https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/WPALXP883507942/LCO?u=usocal_main&amp;sid=bookmark-LCO&amp;pg=203&amp;xid=83113770">combine prose with his poetry</a> in a way Dillard herself does.</p>

<h2>Writing prose as a poet</h2>

<p>In “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-writing-life-annie-dillard?variant=41224246132770">The Writing Life</a>,” Dillard describes the process of writing “a favorite, difficult book” – likely “Holy the Firm” – as akin to writing poetry. She notes that the writing was “so intense and accented, and the world it described was so charged with meaning,” that the idea of going further exhausted her.</p>

<p>To help her write, she read <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/conrad-aiken">Conrad Aiken’s poetry</a> aloud, describing it as “pure sound unencumbered by sense.” She would read a poetry anthology’s index of first lines because “the parallels sounded strong and suggestive.” </p>

<p>She also describes repeating a single line of <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/wallace-stevens">Wallace Stevens’ poetry</a> “for hours, like a song” while writing. </p>

<p>Dillard purposefully channeled poetry’s sonic density in her writing process; it comes as no surprise that the heightened register of these poems made its way into her prose.</p>

<h2>Inspired by ineffable nature</h2>

<p>Dillard’s virtuosic, visionary style isn’t for everyone. Writer Eudora Welty praised Dillard in her <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1974/03/24/archives/pilgrim-at-tinker-creek-meditation-on-seeing-by-annie-dillard-271.html">review of “Tinker Creek</a>,” but Welty also admitted “not (knowing) what she’s talking about” at times and that her writing “leaves something to be desired.” That something was what Welty called “straight narrative,” the clarity of “point, direction, and shape” more often demanded of prose than poetry. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="President Barack Obama with his hands on Annie Dillard's shoulders after placing a medal around her neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=690&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760819/original/file-20260918-50-c1gm6h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=868&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Annie Dillard was awarded the 2014 National Humanities Medal.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-barack-obama-presents-the-2014-national-news-photo/487621272">Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The solitude of the narrator in Dillard’s nonfiction and her apparent disengagement with society also was a source of criticism. As critic William Deresiewicz put it, “There is <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2016/03/where-have-you-gone-annie-dillard/426843/">no economy and no society</a>” in “Tinker Creek.” “We don’t know how Dillard lives, or how she makes a living, or much of anything about her circumstances.” Her mix of cultural disengagement and theological concern smacked to Deresiewicz of “hypocrisy and spiritual snobbery.”</p>

<p>In the contained world of lyric poetry, especially nature poetry, this hermetic perspective would be less of a fault. Her mystical encounters with the divine through the natural world are reminiscent of poets like <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/gerard-manley-hopkins">Gerard Manley Hopkins</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-wendell-berry-meant-to-christian-farmers-going-green-291756">Wendell Berry</a> and <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/mary-oliver">Mary Oliver</a>. The narrow lens of her attention can be viewed as a poetic feature played out at length over her nonfiction essays and books.</p>

<p>Like an <a href="https://theconversation.com/abstract-expressionism-how-new-york-overtook-europe-to-become-the-epicentre-of-western-art-65820">expressionist painting</a>, poetry draws attention to how something is being depicted, not just what is being portrayed. Prose can do this, too – creative nonfiction, especially, and Annie Dillard’s writing most of all.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290676/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>At-home drug disposal products can play an important role in keeping rural Coloradans safe</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757861/original/file-20260903-50-xrd9tk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7360%2C4906&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Unused medications can become a hazard when not disposed of safely.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/high-angle-medium-close-up-shot-of-unrecognizable-royalty-free-image/1361819535">mediaphotos/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Some Coloradans have a drug problem: old prescription medications clogging their medicine cabinets.</p>

<p>Disposing of unused prescription and over-the-counter drugs is important to protect children and teens from accidental or unintentional exposure. Eliminating medications properly is also important to prevent contamination of vegetation, aquatic life and water supplies. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/where-and-how-dispose-unused-medicines">Food and Drug Administration recommends</a> disposing of drugs by dropping them off at a take-back location or by mailing them using a prepaid envelope that is delivered to a facility where the drugs are incinerated. These envelopes are available at some pharmacies and online. </p>

<p>In Colorado, the state-funded <a href="https://cdphe.colorado.gov/dehs/medication-sharps-take-back">Medication and Sharps Takeback</a> program has collected <a href="https://takemedsseriously.org/safe-disposal/">over 400,000 pounds</a> – roughly 181 metric tons – of drugs since its inception in 2016. Medications can be dropped off at over <a href="https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/viewer?ll=39.058162142950565%2C-105.60554450412346&amp;z=8&amp;mid=1VAVgt5_wsMqtDVIYdwjSSpjdBjMDcjI">300 state-funded or independent drop-off sites</a> across the state. </p>

<p>National <a href="https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/drug_disposal/takeback/takeback.html">take-back events in April and October</a> each year are another way to properly dispose of medications. The drugs collected are incinerated and <a href="https://www.epa.gov/household-medication-disposal/information-retail-pharmacies-and-hospitalsclinics-have-or-want">become irretrievable, helping keep the public and environment safe</a>.</p>

<p>I am a professor of pharmacy with a focus on <a href="https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&amp;as_sdt=0%2C6&amp;q=sunny+linnebur&amp;oq=sunny">older adults and medication safety</a>. For over a decade, I have <a href="https://corxconsortium.org/work-groups/safe-disposal/">co-chaired the Safe Disposal work group</a> for the <a href="https://corxconsortium.org/">Colorado Consortium for Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention</a>.  </p>

<p>Although these national and statewide programs make an important difference, there are still gaps – especially for Coloradans who live in rural communities. Let’s look at the different options these consumers have:</p>

<h2>You’re at home – what can you do?</h2>

<p>The FDA <a href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/disposal-unused-medicines-what-you-should-know/drug-disposal-fdas-flush-list-certain-medicines">recommends flushing some medications</a> down the toilet.</p>

<p>This should be a last resort reserved for dangerous medications, like fentanyl patches, that need to be disposed of quickly to prevent them from <a href="https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/accidental-exposures-fentanyl-patches-continue-be-deadly-children">accidentally coming into contact</a> with other humans or pets. </p>

<p>Putting <a href="https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPDF.cgi/P100ZW8A.PDF?Dockey=P100ZW8A.PDF">medications down a sink or toilet</a> deposits them directly into wastewater, where <a href="http://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.145062">they will likely not be filtered out</a>.</p>

<p>Depositing medications into household trash also carries risks, like making them accessible to animals and other people. Drugs can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2016.03.029">leach into soil and ground water</a> groundwater at the landfill.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A pregnant woman throws a garbage bag into a trash can in a backyard." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757863/original/file-20260903-50-bmlh33.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Throwing unused drugs into the trash can contaminate waterways and soil.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pregnant-woman-throwing-garbage-bag-in-trash-can-at-royalty-free-image/2221870093">Johner Images/Johner Images Royalty-Free via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>At-home disposal products are a useful alternative, especially in rural areas where drug take-back programs are not readily accessible.</p>

<p>These products dissolve and degrade, bind up or neutralize medications so they can safely be thrown away. Disposal products come in a variety of different sizes and offer different features, so I worked with staff at University of Colorado Anschutz to test some of the popular brands to see how they worked. </p>

<h2>Pill Terminator test</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://pillterminator.com/">Pill Terminator</a> is a one-time use bottle filled with a powder that turns into a gelatinous substance once medications and water are added. All pills need to be added at the same time. </p>

<p>We attempted adding around 30 pills to the bottle – much less than the stated 300 medium-sized pills that it could accommodate.</p>

<p>We observed several shortcomings. When warm water was used and the bottle was shaken, the powder was fully converted to gelatin and dissolved most of the pills. But there were still some intact pills remaining. When cold water was used, even extensive shaking did not completely dissolve the powder at the bottom of the container. Intact capsules also remained trapped within the gelatin, meaning some medications could still be identified and potentially retrieved. </p>

<h2>Deterra Drug Deactivation System test</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://deterrasystem.com/">Deterra Drug Deactivation System</a> is a biodegradable pouch that uses activated charcoal to adsorb medications after warm water is added. </p>

<p>According to the manufacturer, the system is <a href="https://deterrasystem.com/science-and-research/">designed to deactivate organic medications</a> including opioids, most illicit drugs and vape fluid in different forms like pills, liquid and patches. </p>

<p>Deterra cannot adsorb biologic drugs, such as vaccines and injectable immunotherapies, nor can it adsorb inorganic medications, like iron, calcium, aluminum, magnesium and lithium. Leaf marijuana is also excluded. </p>

<p>Although the product label says to “gently shake,” we needed to shake the Deterra pouch more vigorously to effectively break down the medication. Most medications began to degrade relatively quickly, and the majority of pills were broken down by the water-charcoal mixture. Like with the Pill Terminator, the instruction to use warm water significantly improved the product’s performance compared with cold water. </p>

<p>Despite these favorable results, we observed some limitations: After several hours, extended-release capsule beads were still visible within the charcoal water, standard capsules were only partially degraded, and some sustained-release tablets remained intact. </p>

<p>The manufacturer states that the <a href="http://deterrasystem.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/NIDA-Final-Report.pdf">average time to deactivate 89%</a> of the medication is eight hours; two days for 96%; and two weeks for 99%-100%. The pouch is not designed to be reopened, so after our initial testing, we were unable to verify these claims.</p>

<h2>NarcX+ test</h2>

<p>The NarcX+ disposal system is a <a href="https://www.narcx.com/">biodegradable liquid in a plastic bottle</a>, which can be opened and used multiple times until the bottle is full. It is the only product marketed for at-home disposal of illicit and controlled substances such as fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and cannabis, in addition to prescription and over-the-counter medications.</p>

<p>Initial observations after several minutes showed limited medication breakdown. However, substantial changes occurred with longer exposure. The manufacturer of NarcX+ states that medications become irretrievable in less than two hours, and consuming any of the NarcX+ liquid will cause vomiting. </p>

<p>We filled the NarcX+ bottle almost three-quarters full, and after four hours almost all of the pills were dissolved. At five days, the liquid in the bottle looked virtually the same, with several white sustained-release tablets still floating at the top of the liquid. After a week, they finally disappeared in the dark liquid.</p>

<p>NarcX+ required a little more time than the other products for the tablets to be fully destroyed, but it proved to be effective at destroying a large number of pills – more than the recommended capacity. It is uniquely designed so you can reopen the bottle to continue adding medications to the fill line. NarcX+ is validated for the widest spectrum of medications.</p>
