body: Unused medications can become a hazard when not disposed of safely. mediaphotos/iStock via Getty Images Plus Some Coloradans have a drug problem: old prescription medications clogging their medicine cabinets
Disposing of unused prescription and over-the-counter drugs is important to protect children and teens from accidental or unintentional exposure
Eliminating medications properly is also important to prevent contamination of vegetation, aquatic life and water supplies

The Food and Drug Administration recommends disposing of drugs by dropping them off at a take-back location or by mailing them using a prepaid envelope that is delivered to a facility where the drugs are incinerated
These envelopes are available at some pharmacies and online
In Colorado, the state-funded Medication and Sharps Takeback program has collected over 400,000 pounds – roughly 181 metric tons – of drugs since its inception in 2016
Medications can be dropped off at over 300 state-funded or independent drop-off sites across the state
National take-back events in April and October each year are another way to properly dispose of medications
The drugs collected are incinerated and become irretrievable, helping keep the public and environment safe
I am a professor of pharmacy with a focus on older adults and medication safety
For over a decade, I have co-chaired the Safe Disposal work group for the Colorado Consortium for Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention
Although these national and statewide programs make an important difference, there are still gaps – especially for Coloradans who live in rural communities
Let’s look at the different options these consumers have: You’re at home – what can you do? The FDA recommends flushing some medications down the toilet

This should be a last resort reserved for dangerous medications, like fentanyl patches, that need to be disposed of quickly to prevent them from accidentally coming into contact with other humans or pets
Putting medications down a sink or toilet deposits them directly into wastewater, where they will likely not be filtered out
Depositing medications into household trash also carries risks, like making them accessible to animals and other people
Drugs can leach into soil and ground water groundwater at the landfill
Throwing unused drugs into the trash can contaminate waterways and soil
Johner Images/Johner Images Royalty-Free via Getty Images At-home disposal products are a useful alternative, especially in rural areas where drug take-back programs are not readily accessible
These products dissolve and degrade, bind up or neutralize medications so they can safely be thrown away

Disposal products come in a variety of different sizes and offer different features, so I worked with staff at University of Colorado Anschutz to test some of the popular brands to see how they worked
Pill Terminator test The Pill Terminator is a one-time use bottle filled with a powder that turns into a gelatinous substance once medications and water are added
All pills need to be added at the same time
We attempted adding around 30 pills to the bottle – much less than the stated 300 medium-sized pills that it could accommodate
When warm water was used and the bottle was shaken, the powder was fully converted to gelatin and dissolved most of the pills
But there were still some intact pills remaining
When cold water was used, even extensive shaking did not completely dissolve the powder at the bottom of the container
Intact capsules also remained trapped within the gelatin, meaning some medications could still be identified and potentially retrieved
Deterra Drug Deactivation System test The Deterra Drug Deactivation System is a biodegradable pouch that uses activated charcoal to adsorb medications after warm water is added
According to the manufacturer, the system is designed to deactivate organic medications including opioids, most illicit drugs and vape fluid in different forms like pills, liquid and patches
Deterra cannot adsorb biologic drugs, such as vaccines and injectable immunotherapies, nor can it adsorb inorganic medications, like iron, calcium, aluminum, magnesium and lithium
Although the product label says to “gently shake,” we needed to shake the Deterra pouch more vigorously to effectively break down the medication
Most medications began to degrade relatively quickly, and the majority of pills were broken down by the water-charcoal mixture
Like with the Pill Terminator, the instruction to use warm water significantly improved the product’s performance compared with cold water

Despite these favorable results, we observed some limitations: After several hours, extended-release capsule beads were still visible within the charcoal water, standard capsules were only partially degraded, and some sustained-release tablets remained intact
The manufacturer states that the average time to deactivate 89% of the medication is eight hours; two days for 96%; and two weeks for 99%-100%
The pouch is not designed to be reopened, so after our initial testing, we were unable to verify these claims
NarcX+ test The NarcX+ disposal system is a biodegradable liquid in a plastic bottle , which can be opened and used multiple times until the bottle is full
It is the only product marketed for at-home disposal of illicit and controlled substances such as fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and cannabis, in addition to prescription and over-the-counter medications
Initial observations after several minutes showed limited medication breakdown

<title>Flood-damaged Nepal wants help from the global climate Loss and Damage Fund – but it’s waiting, along with 118 other countries</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760567/original/file-20260917-50-qdglpn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6900%2C4600&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A rush of mud, rock and water inundated the town of Trishuli, Nepal, on Aug. 26, 2026, after a glacier collapsed.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/man-looks-at-the-remains-in-the-aftermath-of-flash-floods-news-photo/2293487411">Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As it faces the enormous task of rebuilding from a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/07/nx-s1-5960357/nepal-floods-questions-over-chinas-reporting">deadly flood</a> that <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/money/2026/09/15/private-sector-bears-bulk-of-bhotekoshi-flood-losses">tore through communities</a> in the Himalayas, Nepal is seeking compensation from the international Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage – meaning from countries that are major contributors to climate change, which it blames for the disaster.</p>

<p>Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said it was not merely a request for aid or charity but a <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/interviews/2026/09/01/this-is-not-standard-flooding-it-is-a-himalayan-tsunami-nepal-s-foreign-minister-shishir-khanal">demand for justice</a> and “legal and moral liability.”</p>

<p>“Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create,” Khanal told the Kathmandu Post. “The <a href="https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/rapid-warming-in-the-himalaya-exacerbates-geohazard-cascades-beyond-adaptation-limits/">rapid melting of glaciers</a> and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.”</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/KrsZ5raaEcs?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The New York Times compiled images from mountaineers and maps showing how the glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Nepal’s US$20 million request is small compared to the <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/money/2026/09/15/private-sector-bears-bulk-of-bhotekoshi-flood-losses">billions of dollars in damage</a>, but it is an important test of the <a href="https://unfccc.int/fund-for-responding-to-loss-and-damage">Loss and Damage Fund</a>’s credibility. So far the fund, created during the U.N. climate conference in 2022 to respond to the impacts of climate change in developing countries, contains a fraction of the money major greenhouse gas emitters pledged to contribute, and it has paid out nothing despite <a href="https://www.frld.org/sites/default/files/FRLD_B.9_7%20Report%20on%20the%20status%20of%20the%20pipeline%20for%20the%20BIM.pdf">requests from at least 119 nations</a>.</p>

<h2>Climate change is raising the risk</h2>

<p>It is scientifically well established that <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/sixth-assessment-report-cycle/">global temperatures are rising</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/ipcc-climate-report-profound-changes-are-underway-in-earths-oceans-and-ice-a-lead-author-explains-what-the-warnings-mean-165588">fueling ice melt</a> and more extreme climate and weather conditions around the world.</p>

<p>Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, largely from burning fossil fuels, have <a href="https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-indicators/temperature">pushed global temperatures so high</a> that sea levels are rising, and shrinking glaciers and thawing permafrost are <a href="https://theconversation.com/alaskas-near-record-landslide-tsunami-sent-a-wave-1-580-feet-up-the-fjord-walls-and-left-clues-for-building-a-warning-system-282017">leaving mountainsides less stable</a>. A September 2026 U.N. Environment Program report determined that it is now <a href="https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/press-release/unep-world-set-cross-15degc-global-warming-can-still-limit-adapt-and">inevitable that the planet will warm by at least 1.5 degrees</a> Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to temperatures before the Industrial Revolution. Communities will have to adapt to increasing hazards.</p>



<p>The world committed under the <a href="https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement">Paris climate agreement</a> to try to limit warming to 1.5 C in an attempt to avoid the worst effects of climate change. But it is <a href="https://www.unep.org/resources/limiting-overshoot-navigating-exceedance">not on track</a>, and many countries are paying the price.</p>

<h2>Is the fund just words?</h2>

<p>At least 119 countries have submitted <a href="https://www.frld.org/sites/default/files/FRLD_B.9_7%20Report%20on%20the%20status%20of%20the%20pipeline%20for%20the%20BIM.pdf">requests for money</a> from the Loss and Damage Fund to help them respond to disasters or adapt to climate change.</p>

<p>About 93% of the requests as of June 2026 involved extreme events such as floods. Over three-quarters included slow-onset events, such as requests for help building the infrastructure, including sea walls, and the capabilities to adapt to sea-level rise.</p>

<p>Together, the requests totaled $2.8 billion – about 10 times the amount of money that had actually reached the fund.</p>

<p><iframe id="yaEV3" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yaEV3/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Map of countries that have requested loss and damage funds"></iframe></p>

<p>Wealthy countries have so far pledged to give about <a href="https://www.frld.org/funding">$820 million</a> to the Loss and Damage Fund, but they have delivered only about a third of that – <a href="https://www.frld.org/nodebim">$250 million to $300 million</a>. The U.S. <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-climate-compensation-fund-withdrawal-0a74bfb4c2b82ed2748f890bb5b604e5">withdrew its support for the fund</a> in 2025.</p>

<p>The fund’s board, meanwhile, has yet to disburse money for any of the requests. At the <a href="https://www.actionaidusa.org/insight/starved-for-resources-the-loss-damage-fund-at-a-crossroads/">most recent board meeting</a> in June 2026, officials considered four requests for funding, but none were approved.</p>

<p>The board has a responsibility to ensure that the money will be used appropriately. But one analysis of comments countries made while negotiating the creation of the fund and decisions of the fund board suggested that the slowness of both the disbursals and the setting up of the fund <a href="https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/frontdoor/deliver/index/docId/132763/file/132763.pdf">had been deliberate</a> – a practical evasion of a responsibility agreed to on paper.</p>

<p>The board is scheduled to meet next in December 2026. Eight of the 26 board members formally requested an <a href="https://www.climatechangenews.com/2026/09/02/loss-and-damage-fund-urged-to-hold-crisis-meeting-on-nepal/">emergency meeting</a> to respond to the disaster in Nepal quickly. The co-chairs of the board <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/national/2026/09/10/climate-loss-and-damage-fund-moves-to-consider-urgent-support-for-nepal">acknowledged the request</a>, but how the board might respond was unclear.</p>

<h2>Nepal needs billions for recovery</h2>

<p>Nepal is asking for about $20 million from the fund. However, the country’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, estimated that the country would <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/china/nepal-needs-least-4-billion-rebuilding-finance-minister-says-2026-08-29/">need US$4 billion to $5 billion</a> to rebuild from the flood damage – nearly a tenth of its national economy.</p>

<p>Nepal lost over 10% of its hydropower capacity when a glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, causing the landslide and flood. Mud, water and rock inundated several riverside communities near the border with China, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing. The flood also broke through several hydropower dams in the Bhote Koshi river basin. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Mud covers a river-side village. The flood spread far from the river's banks, fully engulfing some homes." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760552/original/file-20260917-70-9dgefk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The flood buried several riverside communities in mud and rock and damaged more than a dozen hydropower dams, knocking out about a tenth of Nepal’s power production.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-aerial-photo-shows-houses-at-a-town-along-the-trishuli-news-photo/2291987629?adppopup=true">Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In Nepal, many of the risks come from melting glaciers. The Himalayas and neighboring Hindu Kush mountains together contain one of the world’s <a href="https://www.icimod.org/press-releases/hindu-kush-himalaya-glaciers-losing-ice-at-double-the-rate-since-2000-new-icimod-report-confirm/">largest volumes of ice</a>, but studies show they have been losing that ice fast as temperatures rise, with the <a href="https://www.icimod.org/press-releases/hindu-kush-himalaya-glaciers-losing-ice-at-double-the-rate-since-2000-new-icimod-report-confirm/">loss rate doubling since 2000</a>. When glaciers retreat, the result can create glacial lakes prone to outburst floods and unstable slopes prone to <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-a-mountain-falls-how-ice-and-rock-triggered-nepals-catastrophic-flood-and-why-climate-change-is-raising-the-risks-290779">landslides like Nepal experienced</a>.</p>

<p>Nepal is <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/china/global-aid-heads-nepal-after-devastating-flash-flood-2026-08-27/">receiving aid</a> directly from other countries, but it wants support from the Loss and Damage Fund in part because of what that would represent.</p>

<h2>The symbolism of the Loss and Damage Fund</h2>

<p>In many ways, the fund is symbolic, and that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00139157.2023.2180268#d1e109">symbolism is important</a>.</p>

<p>Vulnerable countries fought through years of international climate talks to establish a principle of climate compensation and distinguish it from charity. Even if the amount that the fund disburses to Nepal is relatively small, it would represent compensation for harm caused by climate change.</p>

<p>Countries are often willing to provide humanitarian assistance, but they are resistant to providing funding labeled “loss and damage,” <a href="https://www.leidenlawblog.nl/articles/loss-damage-fund-justice-or-charity">unwilling to assume responsibility – and potentially liability</a> – for climate change.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People stand on a board to reach second-floor windows of a home. The mud largely covers the first floor." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760556/original/file-20260917-50-twwajf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People in the town of Devighat try to clean a home that was covered by the landslide’s debris.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/residents-clean-a-house-covered-in-sludge-in-the-aftermath-news-photo/2293092565?adppopup=true">Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2026.115300">decision establishing the fund</a> is very clear that contributions are voluntary and the act of contributing should not be interpreted as an acknowledgment of liability. Climate-vulnerable countries consented to that language in the hope that it would bring in much-needed help. </p>

<p>If the fund acts promptly and pragmatically on that shared responsibility, global <a href="https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2025/09/19/law-making-initiatives-of-small-island-developing-states-on-loss-and-damage/">efforts to establish liability</a> for climate change through international tribunals and courts could ease.</p>

<h2>Speed matters</h2>

<p>To be effective, the Loss and Damage Fund needs to be more agile and responsive to the needs of the most climate-vulnerable countries. During negotiations to set up the fund, one negotiator emphasized the need for resources to be accessible <a href="https://enb.iisd.org/sharm-el-sheikh-climate-change-conference-cop27-daily-report-8nov2022">within 24 to 48 hours of a climate disaster</a>.</p>

<p>A coalition of <a href="https://larutadelclima.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Joint-submission-on-start-up-phase-of-the-FRLD-April-2025.pdf">experienced adaptation and disaster response organizations</a> has argued that the fund should prioritize <a href="https://www.undrr.org/news/successful-localization-disaster-risk-reduction-efforts-nepal-supported-through-well">effective existing local and national programs</a> and low-cost and low-risk projects. These include community-based resilience and recovery with local volunteers, health centers and cash transfers to flood-affected households.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ORPDEvHJZpA?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">France 24 used amateur video from along the flood’s path to reconstruct the damage.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>From response to anticipation</h2>

<p>The Loss and Damage Fund could also use its symbolic and modest financial position to nudge the broader humanitarian, development and climate finance ecosystem toward what’s known as <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5125163">anticipatory action</a>.</p>

<p>Anticipatory action involves moving resources into at-risk places before the disaster hits. It has been proven to <a href="https://wfp-evaluation.medium.com/acting-early-the-causal-impacts-of-wfps-anticipatory-action-programmes-in-nepal-and-bangladesh-fea93833208b">speed up the response and recovery</a>.</p>

<p>Emphasizing this approach could also lead to better forecasting, early warnings and planning that takes climate change into account to protect people in vulnerable regions around the world.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291264/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The world committed under the Paris climate agreement to try to limit warming to 1.5 C in an attempt to avoid the worst effects of climate change
But it is not on track , and many countries are paying the price
Is the fund just words? At least 119 countries have submitted requests for money from the Loss and Damage Fund to help them respond to disasters or adapt to climate change
About 93% of the requests as of June 2026 involved extreme events such as floods
Over three-quarters included slow-onset events, such as requests for help building the infrastructure, including sea walls, and the capabilities to adapt to sea-level rise
Together, the requests totaled $2.8 billion – about 10 times the amount of money that had actually reached the fund
Wealthy countries have so far pledged to give about $820 million to the Loss and Damage Fund, but they have delivered only about a third of that – $250 million to $300 million
The U.S. withdrew its support for the fund in 2025
The fund’s board, meanwhile, has yet to disburse money for any of the requests
At the most recent board meeting in June 2026, officials considered four requests for funding, but none were approved
The board has a responsibility to ensure that the money will be used appropriately

But one analysis of comments countries made while negotiating the creation of the fund and decisions of the fund board suggested that the slowness of both the disbursals and the setting up of the fund had been deliberate – a practical evasion of a responsibility agreed to on paper
The board is scheduled to meet next in December 2026
Eight of the 26 board members formally requested an emergency meeting to respond to the disaster in Nepal quickly
The co-chairs of the board acknowledged the request , but how the board might respond was unclear
Nepal needs billions for recovery Nepal is asking for about $20 million from the fund
However, the country’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, estimated that the country would need US$4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild from the flood damage – nearly a tenth of its national economy
Nepal lost over 10% of its hydropower capacity when a glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, causing the landslide and flood
Mud, water and rock inundated several riverside communities near the border with China, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing
The flood also broke through several hydropower dams in the Bhote Koshi river basin
The flood buried several riverside communities in mud and rock and damaged more than a dozen hydropower dams, knocking out about a tenth of Nepal’s power production
Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images In Nepal, many of the risks come from melting glaciers

The Himalayas and neighboring Hindu Kush mountains together contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice , but studies show they have been losing that ice fast as temperatures rise, with the loss rate doubling since 2000
When glaciers retreat, the result can create glacial lakes prone to outburst floods and unstable slopes prone to landslides like Nepal experienced
Nepal is receiving aid directly from other countries, but it wants support from the Loss and Damage Fund in part because of what that would represent
The symbolism of the Loss and Damage Fund In many ways, the fund is symbolic, and that symbolism is important
Vulnerable countries fought through years of international climate talks to establish a principle of climate compensation and distinguish it from charity
Even if the amount that the fund disburses to Nepal is relatively small, it would represent compensation for harm caused by climate change

Countries are often willing to provide humanitarian assistance, but they are resistant to providing funding labeled “loss and damage,” unwilling to assume responsibility – and potentially liability – for climate change

<title>Why the closing prayers of Judaism’s holiest holiday focus on repairing relationships with each other</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760623/original/file-20260917-50-wl2k1f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People attend Yom Kippur services hosted by Temple Emanu-El on Sept. 16, 2021, in New York City.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-attend-yom-kippur-religious-services-with-temple-news-photo/1340731141?adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Each Passover, as Jewish families start the Seder meal, a child asks, “<a href="https://www.chabad.org/holidays/passover/pesach_cdo/aid/4336005/jewish/What-Are-the-Four-Questions-Ma-Nishtana.htm">Why is this night different from all other nights?</a>”</p>

<p>And each Yom Kippur, as worshippers attend the last prayers of the day, they might well ask: “Why is this closing service different from all other services?”</p>

<h2>The Book of Life</h2>

<p>Throughout <a href="https://theconversation.com/universal-ethical-truths-are-at-the-core-of-jewish-high-holy-days-123831">the High Holidays</a>, the 10-day period that begins with Rosh Hashanah and ends with Yom Kippur, Jews pray to be “inscribed” in the Book of Life – <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Unetaneh_Tokef.5?lang=bi">that God grant them life</a>, livelihood, health and moral growth in the coming year.</p>

<p>The holidays culminate in Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement: a day dedicated to reflection, fasting and <a href="https://theconversation.com/yom-kippur-what-does-judaism-actually-say-about-forgiveness-189514">repairing each person’s relationship with others</a> – and through that, their relationship with God.</p>

<p>According to Jewish tradition, the Book of Life is sealed <a href="https://www.juf.org/jewish-chicago/closing-time/">as Yom Kippur draws to a close</a>, as is each person’s fate for the coming year. During the fifth and final service, one prays to be “sealed,” which on this Day of Judgment entails being forgiven. This last service is thus titled “Ne’ilah,” or “the closing,” reflecting the idea that <a href="https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/neilah-service/">the gates of heaven are closing</a>. It also alludes to the gates of the ancient Temple in Jerusalem, where the holiday was once celebrated.</p>

<p>Ne’ilah prayers are accordingly recited at the closing of the day – just at sunset, adding nature’s drama to the closing of the day. The ambience is enhanced by keeping open <a href="https://jewish-heritage-europe.eu/2018/09/30/simchat-torah-rejoicing-with-images-of-arks/">the ark of the Torah</a>, the usually closed chamber at the front of the synagogue that protects the scrolls of scripture. Many congregants remain standing, using this final chance to plead their case as the day slips by. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large cabinet-like structure stands open, containing scrolls encased in silver holders." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760601/original/file-20260917-60-a3cxr8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Torah ark stands open in Garnethill Synagogue in Glasgow, Scotland.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garnethill_Synagogue,_Glasgow_04_-_the_Holy_Ark_in_the_Eastern_Wall_facing_Jerusalem.jpg">Stinglehammer/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>In the image of God</h2>

<p>Yom Kippur is a day reserved for repentance, expressed through confession – and, in many ways, it is a day of repetition. <a href="https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/6577/jewish/Text-of-Al-Chet.htm">The confessional prayer</a> is recited up to 10 times over the course of five services.</p>

<p>It begins with the congregation asking God for forgiveness “for the sin that I have committed before You.” Yet what follows is an extended list of ethical sins, with a focus on the sins of abusive speech, such as slandering, slurring, slighting and smearing the reputations of others. A foundational concept of Judaism is that <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.28?lang=bi&amp;with=Navigation&amp;lang2=en">humanity is made in the image of God</a>, meaning that in wronging others, we offend God as well.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://scholarworks.brandeis.edu/esploro/profile/reuven_kimelman">a scholar of Jewish liturgy</a>, I believe this prayer points to a key theme of the entire High Holidays, and of Judaism itself: that to do right by God, people <a href="https://voices.sefaria.org/sheets/189688?lang=bi">must first do right by each other</a>.</p>

<h2>An outstretched hand</h2>

<p>After reciting the confessional, the Ne’ilah service adds one more prayer, not used in other services. This addendum focuses not on the specifics of confession but <a href="https://www.thetorah.com/article/yom-kippur-demands-more-than-repentance">the dynamics of repentance</a>: underscoring that belief that each person’s relationship with God is correlated with their relationship with other people.</p>

<p>Ne’ilah thus focuses on the sin of fraud, echoing a passage from <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Jonah.3.8?lang=bi&amp;p2=Jonah.3.8&amp;ven2=english%7CJonah%3B_Based_on_Malbim._Trans._M_Atlas,_2026&amp;lang2=bi">the biblical Book of Jonah</a> read in the preceding afternoon service: “Let everyone repent of their evil way by giving back the stolen goods in their hands.” To return to God, then, it is important to return what is owed to other people: emotionally, spiritually and materially.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman stares into the distance as she stands amid other people in a sanctuary." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760632/original/file-20260917-50-tjae8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Yom Kippur involves five prayer services, ending at nightfall with Ne'ilah prayers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/young-jewish-woman-during-congregation-at-synagogue-royalty-free-image/1869577777?phrase=synagogue%20prayer&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Maskot/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Whereas the oft-repeated confessional focuses on offenses of the lips, such as slander, here the focus is on <a href="https://www.thetorah.com/article/yom-kippur-demands-more-than-repentance">offenses of the hands</a>: taking what does not belong to us, such as by exploiting the vulnerable or committing fraud. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Machzor_Yom_Kippur_Ashkenaz%2C_Neilah%3B_Concluding_Service%2C_Amidah_for_Neilah.45?lang=en&amp;with=all&amp;lang2=en">The prayer opens with God’s outstretched, inviting hand</a>, inducing penitents to hand over ill-gotten goods to their rightful owner. But as the addendum has it, God can’t <a href="https://www.thetorah.com/article/yom-kippur-demands-more-than-repentance">hold out his hand in reconciliation</a> until we have reconciled with the people we wronged.</p>

<p>“You give space” – literally, you give a hand – “to the sinner, but You extend Your right hand to penitents,” it begins. “You have taught us … to confess to You every one of our sins so that we cease handling unlawful goods.”</p>

<p>Judaism holds that God won’t forgive you for a sin if you haven’t <a href="https://voices.sefaria.org/sheets/189688?lang=bi">made amends with the person you wronged</a>. During the Days of Awe leading up to Yom Kippur, Jews are taught to ask each other for forgiveness, apologizing for the ways we wronged one another in the past year.</p>

<h2>Repent and repair</h2>

<p>Rather than browbeating people into repentance, the Ne’ilah service’s strategy is to boost them up into it, playing upon the biblical idea of the grandeur of humanity. “You have distinguished humanity from the beginning, privileging it to stand before You,” <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Machzor_Yom_Kippur_Ashkenaz%2C_Neilah%3B_Concluding_Service%2C_Amidah_for_Neilah.46?lang=en&amp;with=all&amp;lang2=en">the liturgy says</a>.</p>

<p>Judaism sees sin as a rupture that can be healed, not an inherent condition. The liturgy’s message is this: Live up to your greatness, your divinely endowed potential, as a being made in God’s image. </p>

<p>For Ne’ilah, the eminence of humanity consists in the ability to repent and set things right before man and God. This is what Yom Kippur is all about.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290744/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>The ethical cases for immigration as a human right</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760033/original/file-20260915-50-2ofgz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People gather in Corona, a neighborhood in the Queens borough of New York City, to denounce ICE arrests on Aug. 10, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/students-activists-and-area-politicians-gather-in-corona-news-photo/2289927117?adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images news</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6072318-ice-arrests-surge-non-criminals/">arrested roughly 50,000 immigrants</a> in July and August 2026; almost 80% of those migrants did not have a criminal record. Until the end of the Biden administration, federal authorities did not expect migrants to leave the country while their <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/28/us/ice-arrests-airports-visa-overstay.html">visa renewal was pending</a>. The Trump administration has changed that policy. </p>

<p>ICE has defended itself for the overall scale of detentions by saying that <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/video/6376522353112">it is simply enforcing federal immigration law</a>. However, immigrant rights advocates are skeptical about this claim and wary <a href="https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/ice-cbp-legal-analysis/">about the lack of oversight of ICE agents</a>. </p>

<p>This scale of immigration enforcement raises fundamental philosophical questions: What ethical obligations do governments have to prospective migrants? And what claims to admission do migrants have?</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/16544951.2026.2618874">scholar of migration ethics</a>, I have studied the arguments philosophers make about migration. Many philosophers claim that immigration should be understood as a human right. From their perspective, governments have an important responsibility to tread carefully when denying entry to migrants and especially when deporting them. </p>

<h2>Freedom of movement as a human right</h2>

<p>To consider the moral foundations of criticisms of ICE, it is useful to first examine the arguments in favor of freedom of movement. </p>

<p>Several philosophers have argued for freedom of movement, often on the grounds that migration should be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199676606.003.0003">understood as a human right</a>. For example, the philosopher <a href="https://www.lse.ac.uk/people/kieran-oberman">Kieran Oberman</a> argues that people have a basic interest in being able to move to any country in which they have core attachments, such as a job or close family members. This argument follows the claim, developed by philosophers such as John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvjf9z6v">that individuals</a> <a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/files/34901/34901-h/34901-h.htm">should be free to pursue their own life plans</a>. They hold that this pursuit is essential to achieving self-realization.</p>

<p>The argument for freedom of movement often involves a comparison to movement within a nation-state. At least in liberal democracies, citizens are entitled to move anywhere they wish within state borders. Political philosopher <a href="https://www.politics.utoronto.ca/people/directories/all-faculty/joseph-carens">Joseph Carens</a> uses this claim when he argues that freedom of international movement is justified as an <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">extension of internal freedom of movement</a>.</p>

<p>Citizens may move where they wish within state borders because this protects freedom. This includes both the freedom to pursue important personal projects and goals, and to pursue <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">joint projects such as business endeavors</a>.</p>

<p>The freedom-based argument for migration maintains that the same considerations that apply within a country also <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">do so internationally</a>. For example, immigration restrictions can prevent people from marrying their preferred partner or from pursuing the job of their dreams. </p>

<p>If we value freedom, we have a reason to allow people to work, study and live wherever they wish because doing so may be integral to a fulfilling life. </p>

<p>If migration were a human right, then any state-imposed restriction on movement across borders would constitute an unjust violation of rights. According to this perspective, then, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/20452610.pdf">states do not have the right to control immigration</a>.</p>

<p>Underlying this view is a conception of human rights in which rights <a href="https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/rights/#RigTru">take precedence over other values</a>,  such as social welfare, because they protect vital human interests.</p>

<h2>Migration and cultural cohesion</h2>

<p>Against this view, other philosophers hold that societies rely for their cohesion on <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674986787">some degree of cultural commonality</a>. In this view – echoed by many political critics of mass migration – unless political communities have shared values, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/opinion/europe-immigration-ceuta-far-right.html">they will be unstable</a>. </p>

<p>A related argument made by philosophers such as <a href="https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/sarah-song">Sarah Song</a> and <a href="https://www.ias.edu/sss/faculty/walzer">Michael Walzer</a> is that <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/immigration-and-democracy-9780190909222?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">control over migration</a> is integral to self-determination. Without it, states cannot be sovereign entities that decide for themselves what shape their society should take. They cannot produce “communities of character”: social groups that share a way of life that they <a href="https://books.google.com/books/about/Spheres_Of_Justice.html?id=2ndITi80AcsC">wish to pass on to their descendants</a>.</p>

<h2>Migration and global equality</h2>

<p>But some philosophers argue national sovereignty cannot override people’s equality of opportunity – a key goal of liberal democracies. Migration <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3366/j.ctvxcrk89">could serve a way</a> to expand opportunities across borders.</p>

<p>In this view, restrictions on migration render citizenship a form of feudal privilege in an unequal world; they deny people from poorer countries the chance to access opportunities and resources <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/1407506?seq=1">in wealthier economies</a>.</p>

<p>This argument holds, then, that restrictions on migration fix a global hierarchy in place, reduce social mobility and give people unearned advantages based on where they happened to be born. Moreover, they do this using <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/228-violent-borders?srsltid=AfmBOoosoO9Ac7ugHlPfw09misdi8x1jWQQ5mSS-Ep6l9Rk14sYSX4EV">all the tools of violence</a> at the state’s disposal. </p>

<p>As with the freedom argument, this claim hopes to appeal to both the left and the right, for equality of opportunity is a bipartisan political value. </p>

<h2>Migration restriction and its impact on opportunities</h2>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a colorful gown sits on a pavement with her belongings and child while making a phone call." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760073/original/file-20260915-50-uoj81q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In addition, scholars such as the political geographer <a href="https://www.reecejonesauthor.com/">Reece Jones</a> argue that migration restrictions <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/676268/white-borders-by-reece-jones/">reinforce global racial inequalities</a>. As Jones notes, the migrants who are denied admission to the U.S., and to Western European countries, are predominantly from countries in the Global South that are majority nonwhite. </p>

<p>Advocates of the equality argument often hold that migration will not merely promote equality of opportunity but also reduce economic inequality. This is because opportunities to access social welfare, healthcare and other important social goods are often greater in wealthier economies. </p>

<p>For example, the philosopher <a href="https://philpeople.org/profiles/darrel-frank-moellendorf">Darrel Moellendorf</a> argues that children should have the same opportunity <a href="https://www.routledge.com/Cosmopolitan-Justice/Moellendorf/p/book/9780813365565">to become a banker wherever in the world they are born</a>. Moellendorf holds that, if there were global equality of opportunity, a child born in Mozambique would have the same chance of becoming an investment banker as would one born in Switzerland. Migration is thus a crucial means of enabling people born in the Global South to <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/24439454.pdf">access lucrative jobs</a>. </p>

<p>There are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780190909222.003.0005">many objections to this proposal</a>. For example, Song points out that different societies regard different opportunities as important. It therefore might not be possible to come up with a global list of opportunities <a href="https://dissentmagazine.org/article/achieving-global-and-local-justice/">that should be equal</a>.</p>

<p>Yet the equality of opportunity argument gets to the core of the dispute about migration. Liberal democracies understand themselves to be committed to meritocracy. This requires that individuals rise and fall based on their own talents. </p>

<p>As migration restrictions deny people opportunities based on where they were born, they may be in tension with fundamental democratic principles.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291118/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The Trump administration has changed that policy

However, immigrant rights advocates are skeptical about this claim and wary about the lack of oversight of ICE agents

This scale of immigration enforcement raises fundamental philosophical questions: What ethical obligations do governments have to prospective migrants? And what claims to admission do migrants have? As a scholar of migration ethics , I have studied the arguments philosophers make about migration
Many philosophers claim that immigration should be understood as a human right
From their perspective, governments have an important responsibility to tread carefully when denying entry to migrants and especially when deporting them

Several philosophers have argued for freedom of movement, often on the grounds that migration should be understood as a human right
For example, the philosopher Kieran Oberman argues that people have a basic interest in being able to move to any country in which they have core attachments, such as a job or close family members
This argument follows the claim, developed by philosophers such as John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, that individuals should be free to pursue their own life plans
They hold that this pursuit is essential to achieving self-realization
The argument for freedom of movement often involves a comparison to movement within a nation-state
At least in liberal democracies, citizens are entitled to move anywhere they wish within state borders
Political philosopher Joseph Carens uses this claim when he argues that freedom of international movement is justified as an extension of internal freedom of movement
Citizens may move where they wish within state borders because this protects freedom
This includes both the freedom to pursue important personal projects and goals, and to pursue joint projects such as business endeavors
The freedom-based argument for migration maintains that the same considerations that apply within a country also do so internationally
For example, immigration restrictions can prevent people from marrying their preferred partner or from pursuing the job of their dreams
If we value freedom, we have a reason to allow people to work, study and live wherever they wish because doing so may be integral to a fulfilling life
If migration were a human right, then any state-imposed restriction on movement across borders would constitute an unjust violation of rights

<title>Pete Hegseth is rebuilding the Army’s ‘brass ceiling’</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759772/original/file-20260914-50-klgx8r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C156%2C4703%2C3135&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and President Donald Trump attend a dignified transfer on July 22, 2026, for casualties of the Iran war.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/secretary-of-the-army-dan-driscoll-secretary-of-war-pete-news-photo/2293012597">Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images News via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/31/us/politics/army-secretary-daniel-driscoll-resign.html">Dan Driscoll resigned</a> as secretary of the Army on Aug. 31, 2026. His departure leaves the Army <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-adam-telle-acting-army-secretary-dan-driscoll-hegseth/">without a Senate-confirmed civilian leader</a> six months into the war with Iran, its <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/us/hegseth-purge-army-generals.html">busiest period</a> since the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. </p>

<p>Driscoll’s resignation was reportedly motivated, at least in part, by his <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/31/us/politics/army-secretary-daniel-driscoll-resign.html">frustration with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth</a>. Earlier in August, Hegseth had <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/us/politics/hegseth-blocks-army-promotions.html">blocked the promotions</a> of four Army officers. </p>

<p>Since his appointment in January 2025, Hegseth has fired or blocked the promotions of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/us/hegseth-purge-army-officers.html">more than 80 admirals and generals</a>. Often, Hegseth has referenced <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/27/us/hegseth-promotion-list.html">“woke” diversity efforts</a> in his reasoning. One officer who was blocked had written a paper while in graduate school about <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/us/politics/hegseth-pentagon-turmoil.html">the impact of political polarization on recruiting</a>. Another officer had his name pulled from the promotion list after officials incorrectly believed that he had <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/us/hegseth-purge-army-officers.html">allowed a mentorship group for female paratroopers</a> to exist in his unit. </p>

<p>More than half of the officers removed <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/us/hegseth-purge-army-officers.html">have been women or Black</a> in an officer corps that is <a href="https://download.militaryonesource.mil/12038/MOS/Reports/2024-demographics-report.pdf">79% male and 74% white</a>.</p>

<p>Hegseth’s blocking of promotions and apparent targeting of women and Black people appear to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/us/politics/hegseth-blocks-army-promotions.html">violate military rules</a> meant to protect against the politicization of the military’s officer corps and have <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/27/us/hegseth-promotion-list.html">undermined faith in the military’s promotion system</a>, which is supposed to be merit-based.</p>

<p>I’ve spent years <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=OadzsIgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;sortby=pubdate">studying the U.S. military</a> and have written a book on <a href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=23msp2tp9780252045721">diversity and military recruiting</a>. In my assessment, Hegseth is building a military that fits a narrow ideological view at the cost of its service members’ safety and well-being.</p>

<h2>Recruiting isn’t ideological</h2>

<p>The Army exceeded its <a href="https://recruiting.army.mil/pao/facts_figures/">recruiting goal of 60,500 new enlistees</a> in fiscal year 2025 and has <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-recruits-joining-military-big-numbers-reason-hegseth/story?id=135546620">already hit its targets</a> for the 2026 fiscal year. </p>

<p>In fact, 2026 marks the third straight year that every <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-recruits-joining-military-big-numbers-reason-hegseth/story?id=135546620">active duty military service has met its recruiting goals</a>. That the Army and other branches have been able to do this – despite the fact that they <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/41675289">rely on women and people of color</a> – would, at first glance, seem to indicate that the politicization of the military has not hurt recruiting.</p>

<p>Hegseth has <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-recruits-joining-military-big-numbers-reason-hegseth/story?id=135546620">attributed the success</a> to “the belief (recruits) have in civilian leadership and military leadership.” According to a <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-recruits-joining-military-big-numbers-reason-hegseth/story?id=135546620">Pentagon spokesperson</a>, “Americans everywhere are prouder than ever to serve.” </p>

<p>What Hegseth and others fail to acknowledge, however, is that recruitment is driven not by ideology but by market factors and need. </p>

<p>Since the end of the draft in 1973, according to my research, the <a href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=23msp2tp9780252045721">success of military recruiting</a> has largely hinged on young people’s perceptions of their chances for upward mobility. Many young people join the military because they are in need of the opportunities military service provides. This past year’s recruitment numbers are likely more a result of young Americans seeking <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-recruits-joining-military-big-numbers-reason-hegseth/story?id=135546620">steady pay, job training and educational benefits</a> than agreement with Hegseth’s vision of the military. </p>

<p>Market research studies conducted in the past year have found that making money, paying for education, travel, work experience and medical benefits are the <a href="https://jamrs.war.gov/Market-Research-Studies/Reports/">top motivators</a> guiding young people toward military service. Recruits are guided by what military sociologist Charles C. Moskos called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0095327X8601200303">occupational appeals</a> that frame enlisting as a smart economic decision rather than by patriotism or nationalism. These kinds of appeals have historically been successful in attracting the diverse recruits – women and people of color – who have been critical to the military’s <a href="http://www.jstor.org/stable/41675289">ability to meet its personnel needs</a>.</p>

<p>Recruiting data shows that Hegseth and other members of the Trump administration have little control over the composition of the enlisted ranks. However, Hegseth’s anti-woke campaign is changing what the military is like for those who serve. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, center, and U.S. military leaders listen to President Donald Trump speak at Marine Corps Base Quantico in September 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20Trump%20Pentagon%20Commanders%20Meeting/189499487cc641cba16423de5aeafcd5/photo">AP Photo/Evan Vucci</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The ‘brass ceiling’</h2>

<p>Historically, women, Black service members and service members of color <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2017/06/07/black-troops-much-twice-likely-punished-commanders-courts/102555630/">have faced discrimination</a> and <a href="https://digitalcommons.law.villanova.edu/vlr/vol55/iss2/6/">violence within the ranks</a>. </p>

<p>Recent firings and blocked promotions have further shaped a military leadership that has historically been almost exclusively white and male. All five service chiefs and 9 in 10 combatant commanders <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/27/us/hegseth-promotion-list.html">are white men</a>. This year <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/us/hegseth-purge-army-officers.html">the lowest percentage of women</a> in 25 years have been nominated to the rank of general and admiral.</p>

<p>This targeting of women and people of color has solidified the “brass ceiling” – a term used to describe the limited opportunities for promotion for women and Black service members – and is creating a military leadership that doesn’t reflect the service members they command or the nation they represent. The overwhelmingly white and male leadership commands an enlisted force in which <a href="https://download.militaryonesource.mil/12038/MOS/Reports/2024-demographics-report.pdf">34% identify with a racial minority group and 17% are women</a>.</p>

<p>By purging military leadership of women, Black service members and those who have supported opportunities for service members other than white men, Hegseth is creating a culture ripe for racial, sexual and gender discrimination and harassment. </p>

<p>Hegseth has also sought to <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/07/black-military-patriots-hegseth/687306/">restore tributes to Confederate soldiers</a> and has attacked military diversity. These actions further erase and invalidate the contributions of women, Black service members and other service members of color.</p>

<h2>Lessons from Vietnam</h2>

<p>The military’s need for more equitable representation was born of the demands and costs of combat. </p>

<p>During the Vietnam War, disproportionate numbers of <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/african-american-experience-in-vietnam-9780742545311/">Black</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230106840_3">Latino</a> service members served in combat and <a href="https://uncpress.org/9781469613895/war-what-is-it-good-for/">were killed</a> while under the command of a largely white officer corps.  </p>

<p>The Defense Race Relations Institute – now known as the Defense Equal Opportunity Management Institute – was formed in 1971 to <a href="https://www.deomi.mil/About-DEOMI/History/">provide race relations education</a> to every member of the armed forces to quell rampant racial unrest, including racial violence and fragging incidents. <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/african-american-experience-in-vietnam-9780742545311/">Fragging incidents</a> – the killing of a fellow service member, often using fragmentation grenades – were rampant in Vietnam.</p>

<p>Army Reserve Officers’ Training Corps programs were <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Black-Officer-Corps-A-History-of-Black-Military-Advancement-from-Integration-through-Vietnam/HamptonII/p/book/9780415531924">instituted at historically Black colleges and universities</a> to increase the numbers of Black officers. The Department of Defense pushed for <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Black-Officer-Corps-A-History-of-Black-Military-Advancement-from-Integration-through-Vietnam/HamptonII/p/book/9780415531924">increased ROTC programs at HBCUs</a> during the Vietnam war as a way to increase the size of the officer corps. </p>

<p>While <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Black-Officer-Corps-A-History-of-Black-Military-Advancement-from-Integration-through-Vietnam/HamptonII/p/book/9780415531924">HBCUs provided large numbers of Black officers during Vietnam</a>, the success of diversifying the officer corps has been limited. Scholars have attributed this limited success, despite consistent efforts to recruit Black Americans, to <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Black-Officer-Corps-A-History-of-Black-Military-Advancement-from-Integration-through-Vietnam/HamptonII/p/book/9780415531924">educational inequalities</a> and the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0095327X16641430">conservative culture</a> of the officer corps. </p>

<p>These efforts were based on the <a href="https://www.womenvetsusa.org/library/library-info.php/num-58/">military adopting the idea</a> that an efficient and lethal military should look like the nation it serves and that its leaders should look like the soldiers they command.</p>

<p>Hegseth’s purging of the officer ranks means the Americans who serve in the military won’t see themselves reflected in leadership or see a path to the top ranks. But they will continue to bear the costs of war: About <a href="https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-08-13/military-women-minorities-iran-war">half of the 18 service members killed</a> in the Iran war between February and August were women and people of color.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290295/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images News via Getty Images Dan Driscoll resigned as secretary of the Army on Aug. 31, 2026
His departure leaves the Army without a Senate-confirmed civilian leader six months into the war with Iran, its busiest period since the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan
Driscoll’s resignation was reportedly motivated, at least in part, by his frustration with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Earlier in August, Hegseth had blocked the promotions of four Army officers
Since his appointment in January 2025, Hegseth has fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 admirals and generals
Often, Hegseth has referenced “woke” diversity efforts in his reasoning
One officer who was blocked had written a paper while in graduate school about the impact of political polarization on recruiting
Another officer had his name pulled from the promotion list after officials incorrectly believed that he had allowed a mentorship group for female paratroopers to exist in his unit
More than half of the officers removed have been women or Black in an officer corps that is 79% male and 74% white

Hegseth’s blocking of promotions and apparent targeting of women and Black people appear to violate military rules meant to protect against the politicization of the military’s officer corps and have undermined faith in the military’s promotion system , which is supposed to be merit-based
I’ve spent years studying the U.S. military and have written a book on diversity and military recruiting
In my assessment, Hegseth is building a military that fits a narrow ideological view at the cost of its service members’ safety and well-being
Recruiting isn’t ideological The Army exceeded its recruiting goal of 60,500 new enlistees in fiscal year 2025 and has already hit its targets for the 2026 fiscal year
In fact, 2026 marks the third straight year that every active duty military service has met its recruiting goals

That the Army and other branches have been able to do this – despite the fact that they rely on women and people of color – would, at first glance, seem to indicate that the politicization of the military has not hurt recruiting

Hegseth has attributed the success to “the belief (recruits) have in civilian leadership and military leadership.” According to a Pentagon spokesperson , “Americans everywhere are prouder than ever to serve.” What Hegseth and others fail to acknowledge, however, is that recruitment is driven not by ideology but by market factors and need
Since the end of the draft in 1973, according to my research, the success of military recruiting has largely hinged on young people’s perceptions of their chances for upward mobility
Many young people join the military because they are in need of the opportunities military service provides
This past year’s recruitment numbers are likely more a result of young Americans seeking steady pay, job training and educational benefits than agreement with Hegseth’s vision of the military

Market research studies conducted in the past year have found that making money, paying for education, travel, work experience and medical benefits are the top motivators guiding young people toward military service
Recruits are guided by what military sociologist Charles C
Moskos called occupational appeals that frame enlisting as a smart economic decision rather than by patriotism or nationalism
These kinds of appeals have historically been successful in attracting the diverse recruits – women and people of color – who have been critical to the military’s ability to meet its personnel needs
Recruiting data shows that Hegseth and other members of the Trump administration have little control over the composition of the enlisted ranks
However, Hegseth’s anti-woke campaign is changing what the military is like for those who serve
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, center, and U.S. military leaders listen to President Donald Trump speak at Marine Corps Base Quantico in September 2025
AP Photo/Evan Vucci The ‘brass ceiling’ Historically, women, Black service members and service members of color have faced discrimination and violence within the ranks
Recent firings and blocked promotions have further shaped a military leadership that has historically been almost exclusively white and male
All five service chiefs and 9 in 10 combatant commanders are white men
This year the lowest percentage of women in 25 years have been nominated to the rank of general and admiral

This targeting of women and people of color has solidified the “brass ceiling” – a term used to describe the limited opportunities for promotion for women and Black service members – and is creating a military leadership that doesn’t reflect the service members they command or the nation they represent
The overwhelmingly white and male leadership commands an enlisted force in which 34% identify with a racial minority group and 17% are women

By purging military leadership of women, Black service members and those who have supported opportunities for service members other than white men, Hegseth is creating a culture ripe for racial, sexual and gender discrimination and harassment
Hegseth has also sought to restore tributes to Confederate soldiers and has attacked military diversity
These actions further erase and invalidate the contributions of women, Black service members and other service members of color
Lessons from Vietnam The military’s need for more equitable representation was born of the demands and costs of combat
During the Vietnam War, disproportionate numbers of Black and Latino service members served in combat and were killed while under the command of a largely white officer corps

The Defense Race Relations Institute – now known as the Defense Equal Opportunity Management Institute – was formed in 1971 to provide race relations education to every member of the armed forces to quell rampant racial unrest, including racial violence and fragging incidents
Fragging incidents – the killing of a fellow service member, often using fragmentation grenades – were rampant in Vietnam
